insider_note: Both sides are already standard Tan⁻¹ integrals, 1/(1+x²) and 1/(1+y²), so separating the variables and integrating each side is all that is needed — no substitution is required.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Cross-multiply to put every y term with dy and every x term with dx.
steps.memory_tip: 1/(1+y²) and 1/(1+x²) are the exact building blocks of the two standard Tan⁻¹ integrals — spot the pattern before integrating.
lines: Given D.E is dy/dx = (1 + y²)/(1 + x²)
steps.why: Cross-multiplying moves the (1+y²) factor to the left with dy and leaves (1+x²) on the right with dx, separating the two variables completely with no further rearrangement needed.
common_mistakes: Cross-multiplying the wrong way, writing (1 + x²)dy = (1 + y²)dx and losing track of which factor belongs with which differential.
Trying to expand or simplify (1+y²) and (1+x²) instead of recognising them as the standard Tan⁻¹ integral forms.

steps.label: Integrate and finish
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Both sides integrate directly to a Tan⁻¹ — no substitution needed.
steps.memory_tip: ∫1/(1+x²)dx = Tan⁻¹x is one of the standard integrals worth knowing by heart, on both sides here.
steps.why: Both sides are exactly the standard integral form ∫1/(1+t²)dt = Tan⁻¹t, so integrating each side directly gives Tan⁻¹y on the left and Tan⁻¹x plus an arbitrary constant on the right.
common_mistakes: Writing the integral of 1/(1+y²) as log(1+y²) instead of Tan⁻¹y.
Forgetting the arbitrary constant c, leaving the answer as Tan⁻¹y = Tan⁻¹x with no constant of integration.
